summary: This specification defines a SIP load-control event package. It lets SIP entities distribute load-filtering policies to others, including rules that throttle calls from a specific user or by source or destination domain.

eli5.summary: When a phone system gets too busy, it can tell others to slow down. This is how it sends those slow-down rules.

questions: what is the sip load-control event package
how does sip overload control work
what does alt-action drop do in sip
subtitle: A way for SIP servers to push call-throttling rules to their neighbors before an overload hits.

tldr.problem: SIP servers can be swamped by predictable surges such as a TV hotline or a disaster, and feedback-based overload control only reacts after the calls have already been sent.
tldr.mechanism: Neighbors subscribe to a SIP event package named load-control. The notifier sends XML load-filtering policies in NOTIFY requests that say which calls to rate-limit, drop, reject or redirect, and when.
tldr.outcome: Calls can be limited close to their source, ahead of time. It only works inside a Trust Domain where all neighbors take part, and it complements rather than replaces feedback overload control.

facts.label: Recommended notification rate
facts.value: No more than once per second

today: RFC 7200 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Load Filtering Next to Feedback Control
sections.content:
SIP servers need load control to avoid congestion collapse. The first approach is feedback control: an overloaded server tells upstream servers to cut the rate of all requests. It is reactive, and it normally affects all calls equally, whatever their destination.

RFC 7200 adds a complementary mechanism called load filtering. It fits best when a traffic surge and its sources and destinations can be predicted in advance. Operators write load-filtering policies saying that calls to certain destinations, or from certain sources, should be rate-limited or randomly dropped. The policies go to SIP servers and possibly user agents likely to generate those calls, and work best when they stop calls as close to the originating user agent as possible. The RFC notes that the idea can also serve other goals, such as service level agreement commitments.
sections.eli5: Feedback control is like shouting stop once the room is full. Load filtering is like telling people at the door beforehand how many may come in.

sections.title: Policies, Computation and Distribution
sections.content:
A load-filtering policy is a set of rules, each with conditions and actions. Conditions say which calls are targeted (by caller or callee identity), which SIP method, which neighboring entity the policy is tied to, and when it is active. Actions say what to do, such as keeping the request rate below a level.

How policies are computed is outside the scope of the RFC. It only notes that a computation must avoid resource allocation loops and should maximize effective throughput (goodput), and that a dynamic algorithm may beat static assignment.

For distribution, each capable SIP entity subscribes to the load-control event package of every entity it sends signaling requests to. The entity that accepts the subscription is the notifier. Subscriptions are persistent, and a subscriber may end one if it hears nothing for an extended time. Proxies learn their neighbors by provisioning or by watching signaling messages.

The RFC gives two cases. In one, a proxy serving a TV hotline sends its neighbor the hotline number, activation time and total acceptable call rate, and the neighbor splits that among its own neighbors, until all edge proxies are informed. In the other, a hurricane overloads a region, and operators configure proxies to accept more outbound than inbound calls.
sections.eli5: Each phone system keeps a list of its neighbors and asks each one to send it updates. When a big event is coming, the word spreads along the chain until everyone near the edge knows how many calls to let through.

sections.title: The Trust Domain Requirement
sections.content:
The mechanism MUST be applied inside a Trust Domain: a set of SIP entities trusted to exchange these policies. In the simplest case it is one provider's network, and domains can be joined by bilateral agreements. Entities must agree on how communication is secured, how membership is decided, which kinds of calls may be affected, and where calls may be redirected. They must also comply with SIP, with SIP event notification (RFC 6665) and with this specification.

Filtering only works if every possible signaling source takes part. A single non-conforming neighbor could flood the server. The distributing server therefore needs countermeasures, for example rejecting excess requests with 503 Service Unavailable as if the neighbor were obeying the rate.
sections.eli5: The plan only works if everyone in the club follows the rules. One player who ignores the limit can still swamp the server.

sections.title: The Load-Control Event Package
sections.content:
The package is named load-control, carried in the Event and Allow-Events headers, and defines no package-specific parameters or SUBSCRIBE bodies. The default subscription lasts one hour, though parties are RECOMMENDED to negotiate a duration if they know their relationship.

A notifier MUST return 403 Forbidden if the subscriber may not receive policies, and SHOULD return 406 Not Acceptable if no requested media type is supported. On accepting or refreshing a subscription it MUST send a NOTIFY with its current policy, or SHOULD send one without a body if there is nothing to distribute. It SHOULD send a NOTIFY whenever the policy changes, at no more than once per second.

NOTIFY bodies default to application/load-control+xml. The subscriber installs the rules and enforces them on matching requests. If a rule's validity starts after the subscription has expired, the subscriber SHOULD still enforce the rule at that time and is RECOMMENDED to re-subscribe. A NOTIFY with Subscription-State: terminated ends the subscription and the subscriber MUST drop the policies from that notifier. Which requests to reject is largely local policy, and subscribers SHOULD honor local priority for message type, the Resource-Priority header and emergency (sos URN) requests.

Updates can be partial. A version number that rises by exactly one MUST be in each NOTIFY body, and if a subscriber sees a jump of more than one, it ignores the delta and re-sends SUBSCRIBE to get a full snapshot.
sections.eli5: You sign up for updates for an hour. The neighbor sends the current rules right away and again whenever they change, numbered so you can tell if you missed one.

sections.title: The Load-Control Document
sections.content:
The load-control document is XML that inherits from the common policy format of RFC 4745, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:load-control. Each ruleset carries a mandatory version (starting at zero, a non-negative 32-bit integer) and a mandatory state of full or partial.

The new conditions are:

  • call-identity with a sip child holding from, to, request-uri and p-asserted-identity. These accept one, many and two new elements, many-tel and except-tel, which use a prefix attribute to group tel URIs, for example +1-212.
  • method, one of INVITE, MESSAGE, REGISTER, SUBSCRIBE, OPTIONS or PUBLISH. Non-initial requests such as ACK, BYE and CANCEL MUST NOT be filtered, and neither are SUBSCRIBE requests for this event package.
  • target-sip-entity, the URI of the entity that originated the policy, so a rule applies only to requests going through that next hop.
  • validity, reused from RFC 4745, giving one or more time periods.

Multiple sip children combine with logical OR, while multiple from, to, request-uri and p-asserted-identity children inside one sip combine with AND. When several rules match, the first match wins.
sections.eli5: The rules are written on a form. The form says who the call is from and to, what kind of call it is, when the rule is on, and what to do about it.

sections.title: Actions
sections.content:
The accept element holds one of three limits. rate is the maximum acceptable requests per second. percent is the share of incoming requests to accept. win is a window size for window-based filtering. For static policies, rate is RECOMMENDED because percentage or window schemes are hard to enforce when load is uncertain.

The optional alt-action attribute says what to do with requests that cannot be processed: reject (default, a 503 Service Unavailable), redirect (needs an alt-target and sends the URIs in a 300-class response) or drop (ignore the request). Over an unreliable transport such as UDP, drop would trigger retransmissions, so it MUST be treated as reject.
sections.eli5: When too many calls arrive, the server can say no politely, point callers somewhere else, or quietly ignore them, but only if ignoring will not make people keep retrying.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main worry is a spoofed notifier. Fake notifications could tell subscribers to throttle all traffic, causing denial of service, so the mechanism MUST be used in a Trust Domain. If a legitimate notifier is itself compromised, other mechanisms are needed to detect it.

The redirect action could also enable a reflection denial-of-service attack. An attacker who spoofs a central policy server could tell UDP proxies to redirect all calls to a victim outside the domain. The RFC addresses this by requiring the Trust Domain to agree on which calls may be affected and where calls may be redirected. For identity fields, a field representing the source of the request SHOULD be authenticated and authorized, while for the destination it is optional.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can pretend to be a neighbor, they can send fake rules. So only trusted neighbors are allowed to talk.

sections.title: Related Work and Limits
sections.content:
The appendices compare load filtering with the telephone network (PSTN), which does similar filtering mostly by manual configuration, with messages naming a control list, call gap duration and control duration. The SIP policy is broader: it covers SIP URIs and tel URIs, offers more actions than call gapping, and allows a future activation time.

Appendix C assesses the mechanism against the 23 requirements of RFC 5390. It meets some, such as graded throttling, and says it must be combined with other mechanisms for others, such as working with elements that do not support it, because it depends on advance configuration and on the participation of all neighbors. Appendix E.2 says it is more proactive than the hop-by-hop feedback approach, which is reactive.
sections.eli5: This is an upgrade of what old phone networks did by hand. It is good for planned rushes, but it should be paired with other tools for surprises.

viz.caption: HOTLINE EXAMPLE DOCUMENT (RFC 7200, APPENDIX D.1, ABRIDGED)

data.title: Load-control document
data.code:
<ruleset xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:common-policy"
   xmlns:lc="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:load-control"
   version="0" state="full">
  <rule id="f3g44k1">
    <conditions>
      <lc:call-identity>
        <lc:sip>
          <lc:to>
            <one id="sip:alice@hotline.example.com"/>
            <one id="tel:+1-212-555-1234"/>
          </lc:to>
        </lc:sip>
      </lc:call-identity>
      <method>INVITE</method>
      <validity>
        <from>2008-05-31T12:00:00-05:00</from>
        <until>2008-05-31T15:00:00-05:00</until>
      </validity>
    </conditions>
    <actions>
      <lc:accept alt-action="reject">
        <lc:rate>100</lc:rate>
      </lc:accept>
    </actions>
  </rule>
</ruleset>
